Splitting a website between a designer, a developer, an SEO, an ads person and an automation freelancer sounds thorough. In practice, the gaps between them are where leads get lost. Here's when one developer who owns it all works better.

Key takeaways

  • Most small business website problems live in the gaps between specialists: a form nobody tested, a pixel nobody owns, a page the SEO person can't edit.
  • One developer who covers design, build, SEO basics and tracking removes those handoffs and gives you one person to ask.
  • You still need specialists for brand identity, big ad budgets and complex software. Hire one owner for the website around them.

The five-freelancer website

Here's a setup I see a lot. A designer makes the pages in Figma. A developer builds them in WordPress or Shopify. An SEO freelancer adds titles and keywords a month later. Someone running ads installs a pixel. And when the contact form needs to reach the CRM, a fifth person sets up the automation.

Each of them can be good at their job. The trouble is that nobody owns the whole website. Every change is a handoff, and every handoff is a place where something quietly breaks.

Five freelancers

  • Five briefs, five invoices and five calendars to line up
  • Design approved in Figma, then reworked when it doesn't fit the theme
  • SEO fixes wait for the developer, who has moved on to another client
  • Tracking added last, sometimes twice, by whoever touched the site most recently
  • When a lead goes missing, everyone checks their own part and finds nothing wrong

One developer who owns it

  • One brief, one point of contact, one person who knows how every part connects
  • Designs made for the platform they'll be built on, so nothing gets lost in the build
  • SEO basics, schema and page speed built in from the start, not bolted on later
  • Forms, booking tools and conversion tracking tested together before launch
  • When something breaks, the person who built it fixes it

Where the gaps show up

None of these are dramatic. That's why they hang around for months.

  • Forms that don't arrive. The form looks fine, but the emails land in spam or the CRM connection was never finished. Nobody tests it end to end, because nobody owns the end.
  • Tracking that double counts. Analytics installed once through a plugin and again through Google Tag Manager counts every visit twice, and your ad results look better than they are.
  • SEO that can't get done. The SEO person knows a page needs a better heading structure or schema, but can't edit the theme. The task sits in someone else's queue.
  • Mobile layouts nobody checked. The design was approved on a desktop screen. The phone version was left to the developer's best guess.
  • Slow pages. Each person adds a plugin, a script or a font for their part. No one watches the total.

from real work: Most of my client work mixes these jobs on one site. For MLB Artist on Shopify, that meant product listings, custom Liquid sections, product bundles, Printful integration and SEO updates. For Luxe Aura Hair, it meant connecting Vagaro booking with website conversion tracking and troubleshooting Meta Pixel events. Same person, whole picture.

Myths about hiring one developer

  • Myth: A specialist always does better work than a generalist. Fact: For one part, maybe. But a small business website succeeds or fails on how the parts connect. Someone who sees design, build, speed, SEO and tracking together catches problems a specialist never looks for.
  • Myth: Relying on one person is risky. Fact: The risk is the process, not the headcount. Staging first, Git backups at every milestone and written handoff notes mean your site never depends on one person's memory.
  • Myth: A developer can't design. Fact: Some can't. Ask to see live sites, not just screenshots, and open them on your phone. A layout that loads fast and gets people to act is design work too.
  • Myth: The lowest bid for each part saves money. Fact: Each bid is cheap on its own. The coordination, rework and lost leads in between are not, and you pay for those with your own time.

When you still need a specialist

One developer isn't the answer to everything, and I'd rather say that up front.

  • A full brand identity. Logo, brand strategy and naming are their own craft. I can build a site around a brand, but a brand studio should create it.
  • Large ad budgets. If you spend serious money on ads every month, a dedicated media buyer earns their fee. I build the landing pages and the conversion tracking they rely on.
  • Complex custom software. A platform with user accounts, payments and heavy back-end logic needs a team. A marketing site, a store or a booking flow usually doesn't.

Even then, one developer who owns the website makes the specialists more effective. They have one person to hand their work to, and one person who makes sure it still works next month.

Is one developer right for your project?

One developer or a team?

Tick everything that's true for your project.

  • The site runs on WordPress, Shopify, GoHighLevel, Squarespace or Wix, or it will
  • You need design, build and SEO basics, not just one of them
  • Leads come through forms, bookings or a store, and you want to know which pages bring them
  • You'd rather message one person than a group chat
  • Your budget fits a skilled freelancer better than an agency team
  • You want changes tested on staging before they touch the live site
  • You also need your tools connected, like a CRM, a booking app or an n8n automation
  • A specialist may fit better Your project sounds focused on one area. Hire the best specialist for that job, and keep a developer on call for the website around it.
  • Worth a conversation One developer could cover most of this. A short call is the quickest way to see what's in scope and what isn't.
  • One developer is likely the better hire This is the kind of project where fewer handoffs pay off: one owner for design, build, SEO and tracking.

What working with me looks like

Every project runs the same five steps, so you always know what happens next.

  1. Discover. A short call or brief to understand your goals, users, platform and deadline.
  2. Plan. Scope, task list, time-box and a clear definition of done, agreed before I start.
  3. Build. Built on staging or a duplicate page first, with Git backups at every milestone.
  4. QA. Mobile, speed, links, forms and tracking checked before anything goes live.
  5. Launch & support. Go-live, handoff notes, and optional monthly care so the site stays healthy.

I'm based in Mindanao, Philippines (GMT+8) and schedule calls around US, UK and Australian working hours, with a few hours of overlap each day for calls and quick replies. You can see the kind of work this covers on my WordPress and Shopify service pages.

Questions, answered

Can one developer handle a bigger project?

Up to a point. A full website or Shopify store usually takes 2 to 4 weeks with one person. If a project needs more hands, I'll say so in the plan and suggest how to split it, instead of stretching the timeline.

What happens if you're unavailable?

Your site never depends on my memory. The work lives in Git, changes go through staging, and every project ends with handoff notes another developer could pick up.

Do you work with agencies?

Yes. I can work under your agency's brand, follow your process and tools, and stay behind the scenes.

Want one person to own your website? Tell me what you're working with and what isn't working. I'll reply with what I'd fix first and how long it would take. Get in touch.
